## Introduction

The general idea was to see if we can use published building permits to identify local projects of densification to see if respondents in our Ontario 2022 survey who have experienced densification in their neighbourhood differ in their attitudes to housing policy than those who have not.

## Backgrounds

Rafael found several municipalities that publishe different types of building permits. The thing is, we need to link the building permits to residents in our survey, so it only makes sense to find building permits for municipalities that are represented in our survey. Here are the most represented municipalities in our data.

```{r}
#| label: respondent-counts-by-municipality
#| cache: true
#| echo: false
#| results: hide
source(here("R_Scripts/1_data_import.R"))

```


```{r}
nrow(on22_building_permit_subset)
```

Of these municipalities, we found good building permit data for Toronto, Ottawa, Mississauga, Hamilton, Burlington, St. Catharine's and Kitchener. If we took those municipalities, we would have `r nrow(on22_building_permit_subset)` cases, essentially stretching across the GTHA plus Kitchener.

### Variables Available by Municipality

One of the problems is that each file collects somewhat different information and stores them with differet variable names. @tbl-variable-map summarizes the variables that are available in these building-permit data.

::: {.column-page style="font-size: 75%;"}
| Variable | Plain-language summary | Toronto | Ottawa | Mississauga | Hamilton | Kitchener | St. Catharines | Burlington |
|--------|--------|--------|--------|--------|--------|--------|--------|--------|
| Permit Type | The kind of permit or application (e.g., building, demolition, plumbing). | `PERMIT_TYPE` | `APPL. TYPE` | `SCOPE` | `WORKCLASS` | `Permit Type` | `FOLDERDESC` | `FOLDERTYPE` |
| Structure Type | The kind of building the permit covers (e.g., single detached house, townhouse, apartment, commercial). | `STRUCTURE_TYPE` | `BLG TYPE` | `BLDG_TYPE` | `PERMITCLAS` | `Sub Work Type` | — | `SUBDESC` |
| Work | A description of the work being done (e.g., new building, addition, interior alteration). | `WORK` | `DESCRIPTION` | `DESCRIPTIO` | `DESCRIPTIO` | `Work Type` | `FOLDERDE_1` | `WORKDESC` |
| Issued Date | The date the city issued the permit. | `ISSUED_DATE` | `ISSUED DATE` | `ISSUE_DATE` | `ISSUEDDATE` | `Issue Date` | `ISSUEDATE` | `ISSUEDATE` |
| Completed Date | The date the work was finished and the permit was closed. | `COMPLETED_DATE` | — | `COMPLETE_D` | `COMPLETEDD` | `Final Date` | — | — |
| Street Address | Where the property is. | `STREET_NUM`<br>`STREET_NAME`<br>`STREET_TYPE` | `ST #`<br>`ROAD` | `ADDRESS` | `ORIGINALAD` | `Foldername` | `PROPERTYNA` | `ADDRESS` |
| Current Use | How the building or property is used before the work. | `CURRENT_USE` | — | — | — | — | — | — |
| Proposed Use | How the building or property will be used after the work. | `PROPOSED_USE` | — | — | — | `Permit Description` | `FOLDERDE_1` | `SUBDESC` |
| Postal Code | The property's postal code. | `POSTAL` | `PC` | `POSTAL_COD` | `ORIGINALZI` | — | `PROPPOSTAL` | — |
| Dwelling Units Created | The number of new homes (residential units) the project adds. | `DWELLING_UNITS_CREATED` | `D.U.` | `RES_UNITS` | — | `Units Created` | — | `RESUNITS` |
| Status | Where the permit stands (e.g., issued, under inspection, closed, cancelled). | `STATUS` | — | `STATUS` | `STATUSCURR` | `Permit Status` | `STATUSDESC` | `FOLDERSTAT` |

: Map of variables {#tbl-variable-map}
:::

## Dates

All municipalities include an "issued date" variable, but only four municipalities (Toronto, Mississauga, Hamilton and Kitchener) have a "completed date". There are advantages and disadvantages to using both.

on the one hand, going with the "issue date" variable will give us a larger sample size. Plus, having building permits issued might actually spur some NIMBY opposition. I feel like it's not unfrequent for neighbours to keep an eye on what is happening. But, building permits being issued might not actually mean that the project was actually completed. My own view is that we should start with the completed date variable and see how well we do. That would give us Toronto, Mississauga, Hamilton and Kitchener. There are `r on22 |> filter(CSDNAME2021 %in% c("Toronto", "Mississauga", "Hamilton", "Kitchener")) |> nrow()` respondents in those cities.

We may end up throwing some of those away as I think it's going to make the most sense to restrict the analysis to respondents who are only in low-density neighbourhoods. We don't really care what tower-dwellers think of densification. The problem revolves around how to get people in low-density neighbourhoods to accept densification.

Some municipalities have building permits that go back to 2017, I don't think we want to include those. The logic would be that utlimately people would become acclimatized to densification, or more respondents than not will have chosen to move into that neighbourhood. I suggest restricting projects to those that were completed in 2021 or 2022, prior to the campaign.

## Residential Units Created

Three of the four cities here (Hamilton excepted) have a variable that encapsulates the number of dwelling units created.

```{r}
#| label: make-completed-dataset
#| eval: true
#| include: false


library(ggplot2)
# Keep one row per permit so units are not counted twice.
# Toronto lists every revision of a permit as its own row (revision_num). The
# unit counts are usually recorded only on the original (revision 00), so keep
# the latest revision but carry over the largest unit counts across revisions.
city.list[["Toronto"]] |>
  mutate(across(c(dwelling_units_created, dwelling_units_lost), as.numeric)) |>
  group_by(permit_num) |>
  mutate(across(c(dwelling_units_created, dwelling_units_lost), \(x) if (all(is.na(x))) NA_real_ else max(x, na.rm=TRUE))) |>
  ungroup() |>
  arrange(permit_num, desc(revision_num)) |>
  distinct(permit_num, .keep_all=TRUE)->city.list[["Toronto"]]
# Kitchener and Mississauga repeat a few permits as identical rows
city.list[["Kitchener"]] |> distinct(permitno, .keep_all=TRUE)->city.list[["Kitchener"]]
city.list[["Mississauga"]] |> distinct(bp_no, .keep_all=TRUE)->city.list[["Mississauga"]]
# Hamilton is left as is: its revisions are suffixes on the permit number
# (-00, -01), usually only the final revision has a completed date, and the
# work class can change between revisions (e.g., Convert Single to Multiple
# becomes Alteration), so keeping only the latest row would lose information.

# Hamilton does not record dwelling units created; add an empty column so it
# can be stacked with the other cities
city.list[["Hamilton"]] |> mutate(dwelling_units_created=NA_real_)->city.list[["Hamilton"]]
city.list[c("Toronto", "Mississauga", "Kitchener", "Hamilton")] |>
  map(\(x) x |>
        mutate(completed_date=as.Date(completed_date),
               dwelling_units_created=as.numeric(dwelling_units_created)) |>
        select(completed_date, dwelling_units_created, street_address, permit_type, structure_type)) |>
  bind_rows(.id="municipality") |>
  filter(completed_date>=as.Date("2021-01-01") & completed_date<as.Date("2022-05-01"))->completed

```

Many of these building permits are in fact permits alterations to structures (think a deck or an interior renovation), but we can't just throw these away as there are variables in these data sets that describe demolitions as well. And we need to make use of that to find densification projects because, a single family dwelling that is torn down and has a building permit to build a new SFD is *not* densification. But an existing SFD that is renovated to add a unit *is* densification. However, just to get a sense of these data, I am going to temporarily exclude any building permits that do not create any units and show some basic summary statistics of what is left.

The scales are really wonky in the distribution because the vast majority of these building permits are for 1 unit, but they do also include permits for a few towers.

```{r}
#| label: units-created-summary
#| echo: false
completed |>
  group_by(municipality) |>
  filter(dwelling_units_created>0) |> 
  summarize(n=n(),
            missing=sum(is.na(dwelling_units_created)),
            min=min(dwelling_units_created, na.rm=TRUE),
            q1=quantile(dwelling_units_created, 0.25, na.rm=TRUE),
            median=median(dwelling_units_created, na.rm=TRUE),
            mean=mean(dwelling_units_created, na.rm=TRUE),
            q3=quantile(dwelling_units_created, 0.75, na.rm=TRUE),
            max=max(dwelling_units_created, na.rm=TRUE),
            sd=sd(dwelling_units_created, na.rm=TRUE))


```

This is a visualization.

```{r}
#| label: units-created-binned-bars
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4
library(tidyr)
unit_bins<-c("1", "2", "3–6", "7–10", "11–50", "51–100", "Over 100")
completed |>
  filter(dwelling_units_created>0) |>
  mutate(units_bin=cut(dwelling_units_created,
                       breaks=c(0, 1, 2, 6, 10, 50, 100, Inf),
                       labels=unit_bins)) |>
  count(municipality, units_bin) |>
  # Keep empty bins so every panel shows the same categories
  complete(municipality, units_bin, fill=list(n=0)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x=units_bin, y=n))+
  geom_col(width=0.7, fill="#2a78d6")+
  geom_text(aes(label=scales::comma(n)), vjust=-0.4, size=3, colour="#52514e")+
  facet_wrap(~municipality)+
  # Pseudo-log scale so the 1-unit bar does not flatten every other bar; a
  # count of 0 sits on the baseline
  scale_y_continuous(trans=scales::pseudo_log_trans(base=10),
                     breaks=c(1, 10, 100, 1000),
                     labels=scales::comma,
                     expand=expansion(mult=c(0, 0.12)))+
  labs(x="Dwelling units created by the permit", y="Number of permits (log scale)",
       caption="Permits completed Jan 2021 to Apr 2022 that create at least one unit.")+
  theme_minimal()+
  theme(panel.grid.major.x=element_blank(),
        panel.grid.minor=element_blank(),
        axis.text.x=element_text(angle=45, hjust=1))
ggsave(here("Plots/units_created_distribution.png"), width=9, height=4)
```

One problem in the data-set is that there are sometimes more than one building permit issued for for developments that include multiple dwellings at the same address; think a new duplex on a block. So, we need to calculate how many new units are created at unique addresses.

```{r}
#| label: units-per-address-variable
#| echo: false
demolition_permits<-c("Demolition Folder (DM)", "DEMOLITION", "Residential Demolition")
# Demolition permits are left out of the sum: Mississauga's DEMOLITION permits
# often record 1 unit, which would count a one-for-one teardown as 2 units
completed |>
  group_by(municipality, street_address) |>
  mutate(units_created_at_address=sum(dwelling_units_created[!permit_type %in% demolition_permits], na.rm=TRUE)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  # Hamilton does not record units created, so its total is unknown, not 0
  mutate(units_created_at_address=if_else(municipality=="Hamilton", NA_real_, units_created_at_address))->completed
```

Then we can filter out building permits that are for larger towers and that actually don't create any new dwellings at an address. I'm going to define mild densification as building permits that add between 1 and 6 units at the same address.

These are 100 random samples in the Toronto, Mississauga and Kitchener datasets showing these projects.

```{r}
#| label: units-by-address-permit-type
#| echo: false
completed |>
  group_by(municipality, street_address, permit_type) |>
  summarize(dwelling_units_created=sum(dwelling_units_created, na.rm=TRUE), .groups="drop")->units_by_address_permit_type
units_by_address_permit_type |> 
  filter(dwelling_units_created>0&dwelling_units_created<6) |> 
  slice_sample(n=100) |> knitr::kable()
```

So you can see that in these cities, there are some building permits for new houses; we're going to have to be more particular about identifying densification.

Plus, we have this problem that Hamilton does not actually have these dwelling units created, so we need to rely on qualitative descriptions of projects in the permit type and structure type variables.

## Densification flow chart

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
  A["Completed permit<br/>Jan 2021 to Apr 2022"] --> M{"Q1: Does the city record<br/>dwelling units created?"}
  M -- "Yes: Toronto,<br/>Mississauga, Kitchener" --> B{"Q2: Units created at the address<br/>(units_created_at_address,<br/>excluding demolitions)"}
  M -- "No: Hamilton" --> HA{"Q8: What kind of work?<br/>(permit_type = WORKCLASS)"}
  HA -- "Convert Single to Multiple,<br/>Convert Multiple to Multiple,<br/>Convert NR to Res." --> Y4["DENSIFICATION<br/>units added by converting<br/>an existing building"]
  HA -- "Residential<br/>New Construction" --> HF{"Q9: Demolition permit<br/>at the same address?"}
  HA -- "Anything else<br/>(alteration, addition, deck,<br/>demolition, services,<br/>non-residential construction)" --> X5["No evidence of new units:<br/>not counted"]
  HF -- "Yes" --> HG{"Q10: structure_type (PERMITCLAS)<br/>holds more than one unit?<br/>(two or three family, semi-detached,<br/>townhouses, multiple dwelling, apartments)"}
  HG -- "Yes" --> Y3
  HG -- "No: Single Family Dwelling" --> X4
  HF -- "No" --> H
  B -- "0" --> X1["No new units:<br/>not densification"]
  B -- "more than 6" --> X2["Larger project:<br/>outside mild densification"]
  B -- "1 to 6" --> C{"Q3: Does this permit create units?<br/>(dwelling_units_created > 0,<br/>demolition permits excluded)"}
  C -- "No" --> X3["Supporting permit<br/>(plumbing, mechanical, drains, decks):<br/>describes the project, not counted"]
  C -- "Yes" --> D{"Q4: structure_type is a<br/>multi-unit or added-suite form?"}
  D -- "Yes" --> Y1["DENSIFICATION<br/>secondary suite, conversion,<br/>laneway or garden suite, multiplex"]
  D -- "No" --> E{"Q5: permit_type alters or adds to<br/>an existing building?"}
  E -- "Yes" --> Y2["DENSIFICATION<br/>unit added to an existing dwelling"]
  E -- "No: new construction" --> F{"Q6: Demolition permit<br/>at the same address?"}
  F -- "Yes" --> G{"Q7: Does the address gain more units<br/>than the demolition removed?<br/>(units_created_at_address<br/>minus units lost)"}
  G -- "Yes" --> Y3["DENSIFICATION<br/>teardown replaced by more units"]
  G -- "No" --> X4["Replacement:<br/>no net gain in units"]
  F -- "No" --> H["UNCLEAR<br/>new subdivision or infill?<br/>needs a location check"]
```

The table below goes through the flow chart decision by decision and shows which variables each decision uses and what it decides.

::: {style="font-size: 85%;"}
| Decision | Question | Variable(s) used | What it decides |
|------------------|------------------|------------------|------------------|
| Q1 | Does the city record dwelling units created? | `municipality` | Toronto, Mississauga and Kitchener go to Q2; Hamilton goes to Q8. |
| Q2 | Units created at the address | `units_created_at_address` (sum of `dwelling_units_created` over all non-demolition permits at the same `street_address`) | 0: no new units. More than 6: larger project. 1 to 6: go to Q3. |
| Q3 | Does this permit create units? | `dwelling_units_created`, `permit_type` | Permits that create no units, and demolition permits, are supporting permits and not counted. Permits creating at least one unit go to Q4. |
| Q4 | Is it a multi-unit or added-suite structure? Note: I checked and Toronto, Kitchener and Hamilton uses this variable to record what a building will become after the project. Mississauga secondary suites are caught in the next question using `permit_type` | `structure_type` | Yes: densification (secondary suite, conversion, laneway or garden suite, multiplex). No: go to Q5. |
| Q5 | Does the permit alter or add to an existing building? | `permit_type` | Yes: densification (unit added to an existing dwelling). No (new construction): go to Q6. |
| Q6 | Is there a demolition permit at the same address? | `permit_type`, `street_address` (searched across the full municipal file, any date) | Yes: go to Q7. No: unclear, needs a location check. |
| Q7 | Does the address gain more units than the demolition removed? This is an address-level test of the net change in units: `units_created_at_address` minus the units lost on the demolition permit. It is done at the address rather than the permit because a city may split one project across several permits (e.g., a new house plus a separate laneway-suite permit, or a semi pair on two permits). Toronto (`DWELLING_UNITS_LOST`) and Kitchener (`Units Lost`) record units lost on demolition permits; Mississauga does not, so we assume one unit was lost. We also assume at least one unit was lost everywhere, and take the largest value at the address so that revisions of the same demolition are not double counted. | `units_created_at_address`, `units_lost_at_address` (from the demolition permits at the same `street_address`) | Net gain above 0: densification (teardown replaced by more units). Net gain of 0 or less: replacement with no net gain in units. |
| Q8 | What kind of work? (Hamilton) | `permit_type` (Hamilton's `WORKCLASS`), `structure_type` (Hamilton's `PERMITCLAS`) | Conversions (Convert Single to Multiple, Convert Multiple to Multiple, Convert NR to Res.): densification (units added by converting an existing building). New Construction of a residential building (Single Family Dwelling or a multi-unit class): go to Q9. Anything else, including non-residential new construction: no evidence of new units. |
| Q9 | Is there a demolition permit at the same address? (Hamilton) | `permit_type` (Full Demolition, Demolish Sgle. Fam., Demolish Multiple Family, Demolition Control; partial, accessory and non-residential demolitions are left out), `street_address` | Yes: go to Q10. No: unclear, needs a location check. |
| Q10 | Does the new building hold more than one unit? (Hamilton) | `structure_type` (Hamilton's `PERMITCLAS`) | Yes: densification (teardown replaced by more units). Single Family Dwelling: one-for-one replacement. |
:::

The next table lists, for each city, the specific `structure_type` and `permit_type` values that count as a "yes" at Q3–Q6.

| Decision | Toronto | Mississauga | Kitchener |
|------------------|------------------|------------------|------------------|
| Multi-unit or added-suite `structure_type` | 2 Unit - Detached / Semi-detached / Townhouse; 3+ Unit - Detached / Semi-detached / Townhouse; Laneway / Rear Yard Suite; Converted House; Duplex; Triplex/Semi-Detached; Multiple Unit Building; Apartment Building | DUPLEX, 3, 4, 5 0R 6PLEX; APARTMENT (\> 6 UNITS) | Duplex Dwelling (2 dwelling units); Duplex Dwelling - Condo; Semi-Duplex Dwelling; Rowhouse Duplex; Garden Suite; Apartment |
| `permit_type` alters or adds to an existing building | Small Residential Projects; Building Additions/Alterations | ALTERATION TO EXISTING BLDG; ADDITION AND ALTERATION; ADDITION TO EXISTING BLDG | none (every unit-creating permit is Residential Building (House) or (Multi)) |
| New construction `permit_type` | New Houses; New Building; Residential Building Permit | NEW BUILDING | Residential Building (House); Residential Building (Multi) |
| Demolition `permit_type` | Demolition Folder (DM) | DEMOLITION | Residential Demolition |

## Diagnostic: Sample of Mild Densification Projects

This applies the flow chart above to each completed permit, then draws a random sample of 10 projects (addresses) per municipality that end in one of the three DENSIFICATION boxes. Every permit at a sampled address that counts as densification is shown, with the branch of the flow chart it came through.

```{r}
#| label: classify-densification
multi_unit_structures<-c(
  # Toronto
  "2 Unit - Detached", "2 Unit - Semi-detached", "2 Unit - Townhouse",
  "3+ Unit - Detached", "3+ Unit - Semi-detached", "3+ Unit - Townhouse",
  "Laneway / Rear Yard Suite", "Converted House", "Duplex", "Triplex/Semi-Detached",
  "Multiple Unit Building", "Apartment Building",
  # Mississauga
  "DUPLEX, 3, 4, 5 0R 6PLEX", "APARTMENT (> 6 UNITS)",
  # Kitchener
  "Duplex Dwelling (2 dwelling units)", "Duplex Dwelling - Condo", "Semi-Duplex Dwelling",
  "Rowhouse Duplex", "Garden Suite", "Apartment")
alteration_permits<-c(
  # Toronto
  "Small Residential Projects", "Building Additions/Alterations",
  # Mississauga
  "ALTERATION TO EXISTING BLDG", "ADDITION AND ALTERATION", "ADDITION TO EXISTING BLDG")
# demolition_permits is defined in the units-per-address-variable chunk

# Hamilton (Q8 to Q10): permit_type is WORKCLASS and structure_type is PERMITCLAS
hamilton_conversions<-c("Convert Single to Multiple", "Convert Multiple to Multiple", "Convert NR to Res.")
# Demolitions that remove a whole building (partial, accessory and
# non-residential demolitions are left out)
hamilton_demolition_permits<-c("Full Demolition", "Demolish Sgle. Fam.", "Demolish Multiple Family", "Demolition Control")
hamilton_multi_unit_structures<-c("Two Family Dwelling", "Three Family Dwelling", "Semi-Detached Dwelling",
                                  "Townhouses", "Townhouse", "Row Dwelling", "Multiple Dwelling", "Apartments")

# Addresses with a demolition permit at any date in the full municipal file,
# with the number of units the demolition removed. Toronto and Kitchener record
# units lost on demolition permits; Mississauga and Hamilton do not. We assume
# at least one unit was lost, and take the largest value at the address rather
# than the sum so that revisions of the same demolition permit are not double
# counted.
units_lost_variable<-c("Toronto"="dwelling_units_lost", "Kitchener"="units_lost")
city.list[c("Toronto", "Mississauga", "Kitchener", "Hamilton")] |>
  imap(\(x, city) {
    lost_values<-if (city %in% names(units_lost_variable)) as.numeric(x[[units_lost_variable[[city]]]]) else NA_real_
    x |>
      mutate(units_lost=lost_values) |>
      filter(permit_type %in% c(demolition_permits, hamilton_demolition_permits)) |>
      group_by(street_address) |>
      summarize(units_lost_at_address=max(c(1, units_lost), na.rm=TRUE))
  }) |>
  bind_rows(.id="municipality") |>
  mutate(demolition_at_address=TRUE)->demolition_addresses

completed |>
  left_join(demolition_addresses, by=c("municipality", "street_address")) |>
  mutate(demolition_at_address=coalesce(demolition_at_address, FALSE),
         # Net change in units at the address (used for Q7)
         net_units_at_address=units_created_at_address-units_lost_at_address,
         densification=case_when(
           # Hamilton branch (Q8 to Q10); Hamilton does not record units created
           municipality=="Hamilton" & permit_type %in% hamilton_conversions ~ "DENSIFICATION: units added by converting an existing building",
           municipality=="Hamilton" & permit_type=="New Construction" & !structure_type %in% c("Single Family Dwelling", hamilton_multi_unit_structures) ~ "No evidence of new units",
           municipality=="Hamilton" & permit_type=="New Construction" & demolition_at_address & structure_type %in% hamilton_multi_unit_structures ~ "DENSIFICATION: teardown replaced by more units",
           municipality=="Hamilton" & permit_type=="New Construction" & demolition_at_address ~ "Replacement: no net gain",
           municipality=="Hamilton" & permit_type=="New Construction" ~ "Unclear: needs location check",
           municipality=="Hamilton" ~ "No evidence of new units",
           # Toronto, Mississauga and Kitchener (Q2 to Q7)
           units_created_at_address==0 ~ "No new units",
           units_created_at_address>6 ~ "Larger project",
           permit_type %in% demolition_permits | !(dwelling_units_created>0) | is.na(dwelling_units_created) ~ "Supporting permit",
           structure_type %in% multi_unit_structures ~ "DENSIFICATION: multi-unit or added-suite structure",
           permit_type %in% alteration_permits ~ "DENSIFICATION: unit added to existing dwelling",
           demolition_at_address & net_units_at_address>0 ~ "DENSIFICATION: teardown replaced by more units",
           demolition_at_address ~ "Replacement: no net gain",
           TRUE ~ "Unclear: needs location check"))->completed

completed |>
  count(municipality, densification) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

::: {.column-page style="font-size: 75%;"}
```{r}
#| label: sample-densification-projects
set.seed(1)
completed |>
  filter(str_detect(densification, "^DENSIFICATION")) |>
  distinct(municipality, street_address) |>
  group_by(municipality) |>
  slice_sample(n=10) |>
  ungroup()->densification_sample
completed |>
  filter(str_detect(densification, "^DENSIFICATION")) |>
  semi_join(densification_sample, by=c("municipality", "street_address")) |>
  arrange(municipality, street_address, completed_date) |>
  # Every row here is densification, so drop the prefix and keep only the branch
  mutate(densification=str_remove(densification, "^DENSIFICATION: ")) |>
  select(City=municipality, Address=street_address, Completed=completed_date,
         `Permit type`=permit_type, Structure=structure_type,
         Units=dwelling_units_created, `Units at address`=units_created_at_address,
         Branch=densification) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

## Maps of Densification Projects

These maps show every densification project (address) in Toronto, Mississauga and Kitchener. Mississauga and Kitchener permits come with their own point locations. Toronto permits do not, so they are matched to the City of Toronto address points by street address. Hamilton is left out for now because its permit shapefile has no locations.

```{r}
#| label: import-toronto-address-points
#| cache: true
# Download Toronto's address points straight from Toronto Open Data
# (https://open.toronto.ca/dataset/address-points-municipal-toronto-one-address-repository/).
# Only the full address and the point are requested, which keeps the download to ~50 MB.
# The geometry column is GeoJSON text, e.g. {"type": "Point", "coordinates": [-79.5, 43.6]}
toronto_address_url<-"https://ckan0.cf.opendata.inter.prod-toronto.ca/datastore/dump/0b3756af-9caf-4f0f-ac28-9c6617adede4?fields=ADDRESS_FULL,geometry&format=csv"
toronto_addresses<-read_csv(toronto_address_url, col_types="cc") |>
  mutate(lon=as.numeric(str_extract(geometry, "(?<=\\[)-?[0-9.]+")),
         lat=as.numeric(str_extract(geometry, "-?[0-9.]+(?=\\])"))) |>
  filter(!is.na(lon), !is.na(lat)) |>
  select(-geometry) |>
  st_as_sf(coords=c("lon", "lat"), crs=4326) |>
  mutate(street_address=str_to_upper(str_squish(ADDRESS_FULL))) |>
  distinct(street_address, .keep_all=TRUE) |>
  select(street_address)
```

```{r}
#| label: map-densification
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 5
library(patchwork)
library(cancensus)
map_cities<-c("Toronto", "Mississauga", "Kitchener")
# One point per project (address). An address with permits on more than one
# densification branch is shown under the first branch in this order.
branch_order<-c("teardown replaced by more units", "multi-unit or added-suite structure", "unit added to existing dwelling")
completed |>
  filter(municipality %in% map_cities, str_detect(densification, "^DENSIFICATION")) |>
  mutate(branch=factor(str_remove(densification, "^DENSIFICATION: "), levels=branch_order)) |>
  arrange(municipality, street_address, branch) |>
  distinct(municipality, street_address, .keep_all=TRUE) |>
  select(municipality, street_address, branch)->densification_projects

# Toronto: match to the address points. Permits write address ranges
# ("1553-1557 BLOOR ST W"), letter suffixes with a space ("718 R OSSINGTON AVE")
# and split "MC" names ("MC CAUL"); the address points use "1553", "718R" and "MCCAUL"
densification_projects |>
  filter(municipality=="Toronto") |>
  mutate(match_address=street_address |>
           str_replace("^(\\d+)-\\d+ ", "\\1 ") |>
           str_replace("^(\\d+) ([A-Z]) ", "\\1\\2 ") |>
           str_replace(" MC ", " MC")) |>
  inner_join(toronto_addresses, by=c("match_address"="street_address")) |>
  st_as_sf() |>
  select(municipality, street_address, branch)->toronto_points
# Mississauga and Kitchener: one point per address from the permit shapefiles
mississauga_sf |>
  distinct(ADDRESS, .keep_all=TRUE) |>
  inner_join(filter(densification_projects, municipality=="Mississauga"), by=c("ADDRESS"="street_address")) |>
  select(municipality, street_address=ADDRESS, branch)->mississauga_points
kitchener_sf |>
  distinct(FOLDERNAME, .keep_all=TRUE) |>
  inner_join(filter(densification_projects, municipality=="Kitchener"), by=c("FOLDERNAME"="street_address")) |>
  select(municipality, street_address=FOLDERNAME, branch)->kitchener_points
list(toronto_points, mississauga_points, kitchener_points) |>
  map(\(x) {
    x<-st_transform(x, 4326)
    st_geometry(x)<-"geometry"
    x
  }) |>
  bind_rows()->project_points

# How many projects could be placed on the map
densification_projects |>
  count(municipality, name="projects") |>
  left_join(project_points |> st_drop_geometry() |> count(municipality, name="mapped"), by="municipality") |>
  knitr::kable()

# City boundaries from the 2021 census
set_cancensus_cache_path(here("Data/cancensus_cache_statscan_data"))
get_census(dataset="CA21", regions=list(CSD=c("3520005", "3521005", "3530013")),
           level="CSD", geo_format="sf", quiet=TRUE) |>
  mutate(municipality=recode(GeoUID, "3520005"="Toronto", "3521005"="Mississauga", "3530013"="Kitchener"))->city_boundaries

branch_colours<-c("teardown replaced by more units"="#eb6834",
                  "multi-unit or added-suite structure"="#2a78d6",
                  "unit added to existing dwelling"="#1baf7a")
map_city<-function(city, show_legend=FALSE) {
  points<-filter(project_points, municipality==city)
  ggplot()+
    geom_sf(data=filter(city_boundaries, municipality==city), fill="grey96", colour="grey60", linewidth=0.3)+
    geom_sf(data=points, aes(colour=branch), size=0.6, alpha=0.8, show.legend=show_legend)+
    scale_colour_manual(values=branch_colours, drop=FALSE)+
    guides(colour=guide_legend(override.aes=list(size=3, alpha=1)))+
    labs(title=paste0(city, " (", scales::comma(nrow(points)), " projects)"), colour=NULL)+
    theme_void()
}
# The legend is drawn once, from the Toronto map, and placed under all three
wrap_plots(map(map_cities, \(city) map_city(city, show_legend=city=="Toronto")), nrow=1)+
  plot_layout(guides="collect")&
  theme(legend.position="bottom")
```

## Filtering Respondents

We restrict the analysis to respondents living in dissemination areas (DAs) with no dwellings in apartment buildings of five or more storeys, using 2021 Census DA data. Our interest is in how residents of low-density neighbourhoods respond to densification, since they are the main source of local opposition to new housing supply. Residents of areas that already contain mid- and high-rise buildings live with a fundamentally different baseline: a small infill project or a proposed mid-rise building is a marginal change to their surroundings, not a change in neighbourhood character. These residents are also likely to differ systematically from low-density residents in tenure, age and housing preferences, partly because they chose to live in denser areas. Restricting the sample to low-density DAs keeps both our measure of exposure to nearby densification and our experimental treatments meaningful for the respondents analyzed, at some cost to generalizability.

```{r}
cities <- c("Toronto", "Ottawa", "Mississauga", "Kitchener",
            "St. Catharines", "Hamilton", "Burlington")
on22 %>%
  filter(CSDNAME2021 %in% cities) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = apartment_in_building_plus_5_pct_da)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  facet_wrap(~ CSDNAME2021, scales = "free_y", axes = "all_x") +
  labs(x = "Percentage of 5+ storey buildings in DA",
       y = "Respondents")
```

## Structure Type Explained

The BLG TYPE variable in the City of Ottawa’s building permit data identifies the type of structure each permit applies to. It covers residential buildings (single-detached houses, semi-detached houses, duplexes, coach houses, rowhouses, stacked rowhouses and apartment buildings), non-residential buildings (retail, office, commercial, industrial, institutional, mixed-use and farm buildings) and a few other categories, including accessory structures such as detached garages and sheds, and demolitions.

The STRUCTURE_TYPE variable in the City of Toronto’s cleared building permit data identifies the type of building a permit applies to. Toronto’s variable is highly detailed, with 187 distinct categories. They range from residential forms (single-family dwellings that are detached, semi-detached or townhouses; two-unit and three-plus-unit houses; laneway and rear-yard suites; stacked townhouses; multiple-unit buildings; and apartment buildings) to a long list of specific non-residential uses such as offices, retail stores, restaurants, schools, hospitals, warehouses and transit stations.

The BLDG_TYPE variable in the City of Mississauga’s building permit data identifies the type of building each permit applies to. It uses a short, standardized list of 27 categories, covering residential buildings (detached and semi-detached dwellings, row dwellings, condominium and street townhouses, duplexes through sixplexes, and apartment buildings of more than six units), commercial and industrial buildings (split into single-user and multi-user retail, office and industrial buildings), and public and institutional buildings such as schools, churches and government facilities.

The PERMITCLAS (permit class) variable in the City of Hamilton’s building and demolition permit data identifies the type of building or structure each permit applies to. It is a detailed classification with 139 categories. Residential types are defined mostly by the number of households (single-family, two-family and three-family dwellings, semi-detached dwellings, townhouses, multiple dwellings and apartments), alongside a long list of specific non-residential uses such as stores, offices, restaurants, warehouses, schools and hospitals.

The Sub Work Type variable in the City of Kitchener’s building permit data describes the specific type of building or structure each permit covers. It has 154 categories. Unlike a pure building-type field, it mixes types of dwelling (single detached, semi-detached, duplex, rowhouse and apartment, often split into condo and non-condo versions) with the specific item being built or installed, such as decks, swimming pools, sheds, garages, signs and plumbing systems.

The City of St. Catharines’ building permit data do not include a variable that identifies the type of building. The closest equivalent is FOLDERDESC, which records the broad category of each permit. Its 14 categories largely follow the Ontario Building Code’s major occupancy groups (residential, assembly, mercantile, business and personal services, industrial and institutional), plus permit types such as plumbing, signs, secondary buildings and temporary structures.

The SUBDESC variable in the City of Burlington’s building permit data identifies the type of building or structure each permit applies to. It has 64 categories, covering residential forms (single detached and semi-detached dwellings, row and stacked townhouses, fourplexes, apartments and accessory dwelling units), commercial, industrial and institutional buildings, and accessory structures such as decks, garages and tents.

## Conclusion and concerns

Mostly this works quite well. However, the Hamilton data might be concerning because it does not actually count the number of units created. The category of `Convert multiple to multiple` might actually include large-scale projects.
